description: Have you noticed that despite our unprecedented access to news, entertainment, and social networks, it can often seem harder to stay informed and easier to feel disconnected? This feeling has a history, and this course follows the rise of the modern media--from the transnational networks built in the 19th century to the growth of broadcast media in the 20th century and the rapid spread of social media in the 21st century. We not only explore the histories of technological change (the telegraph, the television, and the internet), but also grapple with the questions they have raised about knowledge, free speech, social fracture, and the future of democracy. Our daily experience of media is deeply personal, and through reading, conversation, and argumentative writing we will discover why our media landscape appears the way it does and how we can find a stable and healthy orientation within it.
